questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Which smells people around the world like best
How perfume companies create new smells
Why some people lose their sense of smell
Why English has few words to describe actual smells
questions.why: They explain that English is general when describing smells and has few words for the smells themselves.

questions.q: Which smell does Neil say he likes most?
options: The smell of an old leather jacket
A newly opened packet of ground coffee
The smell of the ground after rain
Freshly baked bread from a local bakery
questions.why: Neil says you can't beat the smell of a freshly opened packet of ground coffee.

questions.q: What does Neil say about the words on Michael Rosen's list, like 'funky' and 'reeking'?
options: They all simply mean that something smells bad
They each describe a very different smell
They are only used by poets
They describe pleasant smells
questions.why: Neil says 'all those words really mean is bad smelling'.

questions.q: How do English speakers often describe a smell, according to Georgie?
options: By saying which colour it reminds them of
By giving it a special scientific name
By comparing it to something else, like a rose
By describing how strong it is on a scale
questions.why: Georgie says we often compare smells to other objects, like roses or rotten eggs.

questions.q: Why does Asifa Majid give the example of a perfume?
options: To show that most perfumes actually smell bad
To show that everyone agrees on which smells are nice
To explain how perfumes are made from flowers
To show two people can judge one smell differently
questions.why: She says one person may find a perfume fragrant and another stinky, 'and both can be true'.

questions.q: How are words for taste different from words for smell?
options: Taste words give a shared idea that people can agree on
There are fewer words for taste than for smell
Taste words are more subjective
Taste words are only used by chefs
questions.why: Neil says words like spicy or salty create a common idea we can all agree on, but not for smells.

questions.q: What did Asifa's research find about how often people talk about their senses?
options: People talk about smells more than about sounds
People talk about all the senses equally often
People talk a lot about sight but rarely about smell
People talk about taste more than anything else
questions.why: She says 'we talk a lot about what we see and very rarely about what we smell'.

questions.q: According to Asifa, what do UK parents often do when young children comment on smells?
options: They teach them new smell words
They stop the conversation and call it disgusting
They ask them to describe the smell in detail
They praise them for noticing
questions.why: She says the parent will shut it down, saying 'That's disgusting! Put it down.'
